I am a 54-year-old woman in Ruvuma and I have been farming this land since I was young. I went to school for a few years, so I can read the writing on a fertilizer bag, but I still trust what I see with my own eyes more than what someone tells me. Last season I bought one bag of urea from the agro-dealer and put it on this rice plot, and my harvest was better than the year before, so I will do the same again this season. One bag is all I can afford without borrowing — I will spread it across the plot when the rains start. My cousin in the next village used improved seed last year and her rice heads were heavy and full, so I will buy improved seed too if the cooperative has it when I have the cash. I do not use pesticide or herbicide — they cost too much and I would rather weed by hand. The rains here are usually enough for rice, so I do not irrigate. Between my husband, my children, and myself, we will work about 75 days on this plot from planting to threshing. When it is time for transplanting, I will hire three women for two days each to help us finish before the soil gets too wet, so six days of hired labor total.
